title: How to Train Your Robot: The LanceDB Edition
gist: Hugging Face's LeRobot now reads LanceDB tables natively, letting robot-learning teams train straight from object storage (HF Storage Buckets, other object stores) with a true global shuffle; on full DROID with 8 H100s the remote LanceDB run finished 1.38x faster than a local-NVMe copy with identical loss. The same table doubles as a vector/full-text search and curation index, and on LIBERO, flagging corrupted episodes lifted SmolVLA success from 62.7% to 77.0%, showing data curation, not just throughput, is the lever for robot policy quality.

themes.theme: LeRobot opens dataset layer to Lance

insights.claim: Hugging Face's LeRobot is opening its dataset layer to natively support new storage formats, with Lance as the first, so LeRobotDataset reads LanceDB tables directly without changing recording or training code.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: LanceDB gains a distribution channel into the de facto open robot-learning stack; watch for additional storage formats being added as a sign of a pluggable data-layer ecosystem.
insights.quote: Now it is opening its dataset layer to support new storage formats natively, with Lance as the first.

insights.claim: Robot-learning data historically came in lab-specific recording formats, forcing converters for both datasets and training code; LeRobot's common dataset format and training stack has standardized that ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Standardized data formats lower switching costs and concentrate the robotics data ecosystem around Hugging Face tooling, strengthening its platform position.
insights.quote: Robot learning data used to come in as many shapes as there were labs.
insights.locator: Robot learning data used to come

insights.claim: Converting a LeRobot v3.0 dataset to Lance costs about as much as a file copy because videos are stored as blobs without re-encoding, keeping items bit-identical; datasets without storage_format "lance" keep using the default reader.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Near-zero migration cost removes the main adoption barrier, making fast uptake by robotics teams plausible.
insights.quote: Converting costs about as much as a file copy.

themes.theme: Training from object storage beats local NVMe

insights.claim: Training SmolVLA on koch_pick_place_5_lego (37,972 frames, two cameras) on 2 H100s, a LanceDB dataset read remotely from a Hugging Face Storage Bucket matched local NVMe at 212 samples/s and 0.30 s step time with an identical loss curve (0.324 to 0.107), with 503 s vs 484 s wall clock over 1,500 steps.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Remote object storage can keep GPUs fully fed, reducing the need for local high-speed disk replicas on training nodes.
insights.quote: The GPUs were as busy reading from a Hugging Face Storage Bucket as they were reading a local copy
insights.locator: Two H100s on this model consume

insights.claim: On full DROID (27,630,375 frames, 95,658 episodes, 369 GB of video) training SmolVLA for 10,000 steps on 8 H100s, LanceDB over a remote object store finished in 1h27m vs 2h00m for LeRobot's standard reader on local NVMe (1.38x faster), with 495 vs 361 samples/s and identical final loss of 0.2380.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Data loading, not compute, was a major bottleneck; better data layers raise effective GPU utilization and cut training cost per run.

insights.claim: With the standard local-NVMe reader, GPUs spent 37.4% of time waiting on data during DROID training versus 1.7% with LanceDB over object storage, and the local run also required a 384 GB download first.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Over a third of expensive GPU time can be idle on data I/O in robotics training; data infrastructure is a direct lever on GPU ROI.
insights.quote: The loss curves matched to four decimal places at every step, so the 33-minute gap is time the GPUs spent waiting for data.
insights.locator: The loss curves matched to four

insights.claim: In standalone loader benchmarks across six public datasets, LanceDB was 1.7x faster than LeRobot's streaming reader on DROID using a fraction of the RAM and up to 11.6x faster on others, and its remote global shuffle was 1.1x to 1.7x faster than upstream reading a local copy.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Gains vary with dataset size and camera/metadata complexity; the comparison is against a streaming reader still under active development, so the gap may narrow.
insights.quote: This implementation is under active development, so the comparison reflects the version tested.

insights.claim: Hugging Face Storage Buckets provide Hub-native object storage addressable via hf://buckets paths and the hf CLI, positioned as the place to keep robotics datasets too large to replicate across every machine.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Hugging Face is moving into large-scale data storage, a potential revenue line competing with general cloud object stores for AI/robotics data.

themes.theme: One table as training data and search index

insights.claim: Parquet+MP4 robotics pipelines require about four systems kept in sync (vector database, search service, metrics table, manifest) because Parquet lacks secondary indexes, whereas a single LanceDB table holds embeddings, full-text indexes and derived scores as columns the trainer reads at a pinned version.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Consolidation pitch threatens standalone vector databases and search services in the AI-data stack; watch multimodal lakehouse formats absorbing those roles.
insights.quote: Parquet stores columns well but has no secondary indexes, such as no vector index, no full-text index, nothing to find frames with except a scan.
insights.locator: The training table is also the search index

insights.claim: With LanceDB Enterprise, a new feature column is declared and backfilled without rewriting data; adding a jerk_score to DROID grew the table by 7% while readers pinned to the old version kept working.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Schema evolution without copies is a monetizable enterprise feature, pointing to LanceDB's commercial model around the open format.
insights.locator: Add a feature without copying the dataset

insights.claim: A GPU UDF embedded 610,403 DROID frames with SigLIP2 at 712 frames/s on 2 GPUs, reading directly from the video blob column without a local copy.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: In-place embedding at scale makes visual search over robot data practical, increasing demand for GPU compute for data curation, not only training.

insights.claim: Visual nearest-neighbor mining on image embeddings found the same real-world behavior (manipulating soft fabric) in 5 of 8 results across different homes, while 0 of 8 were exact text matches, showing text instructions are an unreliable index for robot behavior.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Embedding-based search is needed to mine unlabeled robot behavior, supporting demand for multimodal indexing tools.
insights.quote: Text search for duvet would miss most of these examples. Visual similarity finds them even when people use different words.

insights.claim: Inspecting a DROID episode in Foxglove directly from object storage pulled 132.7 MB over 54 seconds of playback, just 0.036% of the 369 GB dataset.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Byte-range access cuts egress and storage duplication costs for TB-scale robotics datasets.
insights.locator: Inspect episodes without moving the data

themes.theme: Hidden flaws in DROID and common filters

insights.claim: The common 'smoothness' quality filter for robot data points the wrong way: across 95,603 DROID episodes, successful episodes were jerkier than failed ones (AUROC 0.402), so filtering jerky episodes removes good data.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Popular heuristic curation can degrade robot policies; teams with data-driven curation tools may gain an edge.
insights.quote: The usual "smoothness" quality filter points the wrong way.

insights.claim: DROID's default 80/20 train/eval split leaks information because all 72 buildings and all 78 collectors appear in both training and validation sets.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Reported generalization results on DROID may be overstated; discount benchmark claims built on the default split.
insights.quote: The default train/eval split leaks information.

insights.claim: OpenPI's 'idle filter' removes 11.66% of DROID, and its released source hard-codes the post-filter dataset length instead of computing it.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Widely used robot-policy pipelines contain brittle data-handling assumptions, a reproducibility risk for results built on them.

insights.claim: On LIBERO (1,693 demos, 40 tasks), corrupting 30% of episodes via swapped instructions, action noise and 0.6 s action misalignment dropped SmolVLA overall success from 86.0% to 62.7%; filtering flagged episodes restored it to 77.0%, near the 80.2% perfect-removal ceiling.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Data quality swings robot policy success by over 20 points, making data curation tooling a high-value layer in the robotics AI stack.
insights.quote: Corruption dropped overall success from 86.0% to 62.7%. Filtering the flagged episodes brought it back to 77.0%, close to the 80.2% ceiling.

insights.claim: Simple per-episode quality scores (goal_dist, jerk_score, act_lag) detected corrupted robot demonstrations at 96% precision and 93% recall, with most misses being wrong labels on tasks whose final frames look nearly identical; on the LIBERO Goal suite success recovered from 48% to 85%.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Cheap automated detectors can recover most of the damage from messy teleoperation data, reducing reliance on costly manual review.
insights.quote: The checks ran at 96% precision and 93% recall.

insights.claim: On DROID, SmolVLA's next-action mean absolute error on 48 held-out episodes fell from 0.3259 to 0.1004 after 10,000 steps, with all 48 episodes improving across different levels of arm motion.
insights.speaker: Caroline Pascal
insights.so_what: Small open VLA models trained on open robot data are learning meaningfully in short runs, lowering the barrier for robotics entrants.
